title: A cache simulator: writes, and when memory finds out

prereqs.why: The whole of `decode` is this: which bits are the offset, which are the index, and what is left.
Each field is one shift and one mask, and the mask for a zero-width field is the case that catches people.
Three files are compiled separately and linked, so a signature that does not match its declaration is a link error rather than a compile error.
The victim is still chosen by least-recently-used; what changes is what throwing it out costs.
Write-allocate and write-back are the two policies being implemented, and the counting rule follows from them.

statement:
**Milestone 3 of 3.** Writes, and the only question a cache really has
to answer about them: when does the data go back to memory?

### What is new

One more command and one more counter.

```
decode <addr>   print  tag=<t> index=<i> offset=<o>
read <addr>     print  hit  or  miss
write <addr>    print  hit  or  miss
stats           print  <hits> hits, <misses> misses, <evictions> evictions, <writebacks> writebacks
```

The header gains two methods:

```cpp
bool write(std::uint64_t addr);
std::size_t writebacks() const;
```

### The policy, exactly

This cache is **write-allocate** and **write-back**.

- **Write-allocate.** A write that misses brings the block in first,
  exactly as a read would — same eviction, same LRU bookkeeping — and
  then writes it. So it counts as a miss, and `write` returns `false`.
- **Write-back.** A written line is *dirty*: memory no longer agrees
  with it. Nothing goes to memory at the time of the write.
- A dirty line being **evicted** is one writeback. A clean line being
  evicted is not. Filling a way that was never used is neither an
  eviction nor a writeback.
- A line that arrives by a **read** is clean. A line that is replaced
  starts again from clean, whatever was in it before.
- `write` returns `true` when the block was already present. That is a
  hit, it counts as a hit, and the line becomes dirty if it was not
  already.

### The sample

```
1 1 16
write 0     ->  miss     allocate, then write: the line is dirty
write 0     ->  hit      still dirty
read 100    ->  miss     evicts a dirty line: one writeback
read 0      ->  miss     evicts a CLEAN line: no writeback
stats       ->  1 hits, 3 misses, 2 evictions, 1 writebacks
```

### Carrying your work forward

Your `include/cache.hpp` and `src/cache.cpp` come with you from
milestone 2, with the same rule as before: a file you edited stays
yours, a file you never touched is replaced by this milestone's version.

If you kept your own header, it does not declare `write` or
`writebacks`, and `main.cpp` will not link until it does — the linker
will name the missing symbol. If you kept your own `src/cache.cpp`, it
has no `Cache::write` in it, and that is a **link** error rather than a
compile error, because the two files are compiled separately and neither
of them is wrong on its own.
hints: A write is a read that leaves the line dirty. Do not write the lookup twice: call the read path, then find the line it left behind and set its flag.
The dirty bit is per line, not per set and not per cache. It is set by a write and cleared when the line is replaced — a block arriving from memory is identical to memory until somebody writes it.

Count the writeback at the same moment you count the eviction, and only there: look at the victim's dirty flag before you overwrite it. Afterwards is too late, and it is the most common way to get this wrong.
`read 0 / read 100 / read 0` on a one-way cache evicts twice and writes back nothing. If your writebacks are not zero there, you are counting evictions rather than dirty evictions.
